rules.instruction: When the description ends the process with a sentence in which a participant carries out a further described activity after the last stated step, and that activity is an action the flow still has to perform, not a received message or a state that is merely reached: Model that final performed activity as a task placed before the end event, in the performer's lane or pool when one is given. Close the flow with a plain end event whose name does not repeat the activity or its result. Do not use the end event to stand for the performed activity, and do not drop the activity from the model.
rules.situation: the description ends the process with a sentence in which a participant carries out a further described activity after the last stated step, and that activity is an action the flow still has to perform, not a received message or a state that is merely reached

rules.instruction: When the description opens with a participant performing an action that is itself a described step of the process, so the action could be read as the process trigger: Model a plain start event that marks the beginning of the process, followed by a task labelled with the described action. Do not use the start event itself to represent the performed action, and do not omit the action from the model.
rules.situation: the description's first sentence has a participant performing a work activity (such as preparing or drafting something) rather than naming an external event, message, time or condition that starts the process

rules.instruction: When the description states that a plan may go through several rounds of review, that each adjustment made after a review is documented and approved by stakeholders, and that a later step follows once the final version is approved: Model each adjustment made after a review as its own task, followed by a sequence flow into a separate approval task for that adjustment. Connect the approval task back to the review cycle, so that further rounds can follow, and leave the cycle through the decision on whether another round is needed. Model the approval of the final version as its own task with a sequence flow to the next stated step, so that no approved outcome is left without an outgoing flow.
rules.situation: the description states that a plan may go through several rounds of review, that each adjustment made after a review is documented and approved by stakeholders, and that a later step follows once the final version is approved

rules.instruction: When the description states that a participant performs an action that is a step of the process, such as communicating an outcome to another party or collecting feedback from a party, and that action happens on only one branch of a decision or after the main work is done: Model each such performed action as a task, placed on every branch where the description states it occurs and in the order the description gives. Do not replace the performed action with an intermediate throw or catch event. Reserve intermediate events for occurrences the process waits for or reacts to.
rules.situation: the description says that a review or assessment gives feedback, and that this feedback is the basis for a later decision on whether a revision is made, so the feedback reaches the decision through the people who give it

rules.instruction: When the description states that, between two steps of the sequence, a further action is performed on the work product (for example recording it or obtaining approval for it) before the next step begins: Model each such explicitly stated action as its own task placed between the two neighbouring steps, connected by sequence flows, and do not link the neighbouring tasks directly.
rules.situation: the description states that, between two steps of the sequence, a further action is performed on the work product (for example recording it or obtaining approval for it) before the next step begins

rules.instruction: Do not merge separately described actions into one task or split one stated action without a process reason. Preserve described dependencies.
rules.situation: the description joins two distinct actions performed on the same object with 'and' (for example, one action that records an item and another that approves it), and a later sentence states a further action on the result

promoted.trigger: the description states that a work item may be revised over several review cycles, that each revision is recorded and approved by responsible parties, and that a later step follows once the final approved state is reached
promoted.instruction: Model each revision made after a review as its own task, followed by a sequence flow into a separate approval task for that revision. Connect the approval task back to the review cycle so that further cycles can follow, and exit the cycle through a gateway that decides whether another cycle is needed. Model the approval of the final state as its own task with a sequence flow to the next stated step, so that no approved outcome lacks an outgoing flow.
promoted.detail: general form of EXS-025, written after it improved the model of example 14
